author: John T. Morse Jr.
claims: The Second Inaugural Address was delivered from the eastern portico of the Capitol.
Lincoln's anxiety before his second term was that the North, in a severe or vindictive temper, might deal too harshly with a conquered South, thus perpetuating sectional antagonism.

Lincoln viewed his call to a second term as an expression of public judgment that he could better finish the difficult work of restoring the Union, having been schooled by four years of national peril.
In Lincoln's opinion, mere conquest was not the completion of the difficult work of restoring the Union.
Lincoln submitted a draft to his cabinet on the evening of February 5, covering points related to reconciliation, but it was unanimously disapproved.
Secretary Welles remarked that there could be such a thing as overdoing a measure to the point of causing distrust or adverse feeling.
It was believed that Lincoln's reconciliation proposition would likely not pass Congress and could be misconstrued by the rebels if offered.
Scarcely any Republican was ready to meet the rebels with the free and ample forgiveness Lincoln desired to offer.
Later opinion suggested that Lincoln's schemes for reconciliation were impracticable.
The fourth of March was close at hand, when Lincoln was to address the people for the second time.
The black and appalling cloud of war that had hung oppressively over the country four years prior was now passing away.
